newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 99 -1 on last week
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 133 n/c on last week
AMLC COMMENTARY: Cattle and sheep yardings eased from the massive numbers of last week, but in the case of cattle this did not stop prices from falling.

Despite the easing in yardings, they remain historically high. At livestock market reporting centres in Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria over 61,600 head were yarded, compared with last April's average weekly rate of 41,300 head.

Processing levels were extreme in the two largest beef producing states last week. The Queensland cattle kill was over 60,000 head, the highest since September 1995. In New South Wales, in excess of 47,000 cattle were slaughtered, the heaviest weekly kill since October 1994.

The other dampener on cattle prices this week was the subdued export trading environment. Prices eased 1-2 USc/lb for manufacturing beef in the U.S. as offers of imported product, especially out of New Zealand, increased. The rise in fed cattle prices over the week has, for the moment, largely priced chucks out of grinding mixes. A rise in retail demand, by driving higher wholesale beef prices, was largely responsible for this price increase.

The United States Department of Agriculture's (USDA) cattle on feed report due out tonight should confirm the maintenance of large feedlot supplies. U.S. analysts are united in expecting cattle on feed numbers to be around eight percent higher than year ago levels. The bulk of these large U.S. feedlot inventories will hit the market during the northern hemisphere late spring/summer (May to August)

Across the Pacific, prices in the Japanese market largely remained flat this week as poor consumption levels resist a recovery in this market. Lower consumption in Japan has not only been confined to beef.

A closer look at Australia's exports to Japan, which were down by 4.7 percent over the first quarter of 1997, shows that the majority of the decline occured in the chilled grainfed proportion, which fell 19.4 percent or 4500 tonnes on 1996. One reason for this is the increased use of chill grainfed U.S. product, as Japanese frozen inventories are whittled down.
